title: The Human Microglial HMC3 Cell Line: Current Status, Experimental Utility, and Future Directions

subsections.section_title: Historical Development, Identity, and Nomenclature of the HMC3 Cell Line
subsections.content:
The HMC3 lineage originated from primary human embryonic brain–derived microglia established as an in vitro model to study human microglial biology. The foundational report by Janabi and colleagues described isolation of human fetal microglial cells and their immortalization using simian virus 40 (SV40) large T antigen, generating a continuously proliferating line that retained a number of microglia-associated morphological and functional properties in culture, including responsiveness to inflammatory stimuli and phagocytic activity ref [1]. This work was significant because it provided one of the earliest renewable human microglial models at a time when access to primary human microglia was highly limited.

The cell line later became widely disseminated through ATCC, where it is catalogued as HMC3 (CRL-3304). However, many studies have traced this repository line to the same historical lineage long referred to in the literature as CHME3 or CHME-3, creating a persistent ambiguity between original derivation, later naming, and repository standardization. Comparative discussion in the microglial-model literature has therefore treated HMC3 as a human immortalized microglial line of fetal origin whose establishment predates its modern repository designation ref [2], ref [3].

For survey purposes, the key point is that HMC3 emerged from early efforts to create a stable human microglial surrogate rather than from recent stem-cell engineering or acute primary isolation. Its establishment solved a practical bottleneck in experimental neuroimmunology, but the historical layering of derivation, immortalization, and renaming has made careful reconstruction of origin essential when interpreting older and newer studies that may be referring to the same biological lineage under different labels.

subsections.section_title: Historical Development, Identity, and Nomenclature of the HMC3 Cell Line
subsections.subsection_title: Nomenclature and synonymy in the literature
subsections.content:
A persistent source of confusion in the HMC3 literature is the coexistence of several names for what is generally treated as the same immortalized human fetal microglial line. The original reports described an immortalized human fetal brain–derived microglial cell line generated with SV40 large T antigen and commonly referred to as HMC3 or “human microglia clone 3” ref [4]. Subsequent papers, however, often used related labels such as CHME3/CHME-3, and in some cases authors discussed the line without clearly distinguishing clone designations from broader laboratory naming conventions.

This synonymy became more entrenched as the cell line entered repositories and secondary use. The ATCC deposit is catalogued as HMC3 (CRL-3304), yet many recent studies still cite earlier work performed under the CHME3 designation or use the two names interchangeably, complicating literature searches and cross-study comparison ref [5], ref [6]. In practice, this means that datasets attributed to HMC3 should be interpreted with attention to provenance, source repository, and passage history rather than to nomenclature alone.

Because naming drift can obscure whether investigators used the same biological material, careful reporting is essential. At minimum, studies should specify the exact repository identifier, original naming used by the supplier or publication, and any stated relationship between HMC3 and CHME3. Such explicit annotation is particularly important in microglial research, where immortalized lines already differ substantially from primary or stem-cell-derived human microglia and where ambiguous naming can further undermine reproducibility.

subsections.section_title: Historical Development, Identity, and Nomenclature of the HMC3 Cell Line
subsections.subsection_title: Immortalization and consequences for cellular behavior
subsections.content:
A key interpretive issue for HMC3 is that it is an immortalized human microglial line rather than a primary, terminally differentiated microglial preparation. Human microglia used to establish this model were immortalized with the SV40 large T antigen, a manipulation that supports long-term propagation but also rewires cell-cycle control and can alter differentiation state, signaling thresholds, and stress responses ref [7]. More broadly, experience with immortalized human microglial systems has shown that indefinite growth often comes at the cost of partial divergence from the transcriptional and functional phenotypes seen in ex vivo adult microglia ref [8].

For HMC3 specifically, immortalization helps explain both its practical value and its limitations. The line is easy to expand, experimentally tractable, and more reproducible than donor-derived primary cultures, which has encouraged its use in neuroinflammation, infection, and neurodegeneration studies. At the same time, immortalized microglia may display attenuated homeostatic programs, altered cytokine output, non-physiologic proliferative behavior, and incomplete recapitulation of the ramified, tissue-imprinted state that characterizes resident human microglia in the CNS ref [2,3]. Consequently, findings obtained in HMC3 are often best interpreted as reflecting a convenient transformed microglial-like model rather than a full surrogate for adult human microglia.

These caveats are particularly important when comparing HMC3 with newer human iPSC-derived or acutely isolated microglial models, which better preserve canonical microglial markers and niche-dependent phenotypes ref [3,4]. In survey terms, the immortalization step is therefore not a minor technical detail but a central determinant of how HMC3 behaves, what questions it can answer reliably, and where orthogonal validation in more physiological systems is needed.

subsections.section_title: Historical Development, Identity, and Nomenclature of the HMC3 Cell Line
subsections.content:
Authentication and provenance are recurrent concerns for HMC3 because the line has circulated under multiple names and through secondary redistribution rather than a single continuously updated primary source. The original human microglial culture was described by Janabi and colleagues, who established an SV40 large T antigen-immortalized fetal brain-derived microglial line that later became associated with the HMC3 designation in repositories and subsequent literature ref [11]. This historical separation between original publication and later repository naming has contributed to ambiguity in how investigators report the model.

Repository records have therefore become especially important for standardization. The American Type Culture Collection lists HMC3 as ATCC® CRL-3304™ and explicitly links it to the historical designation CHME3, providing a practical anchor for provenance, basic growth conditions, and identity claims used in contemporary studies ref [12]. In surveying the literature, authors should distinguish experiments performed with authenticated ATCC stocks from work using locally maintained or third-party shared cultures, because passage history and undocumented relabeling can complicate cross-study comparison.

More broadly, the need for rigorous authentication in glial and neural cell models has been emphasized by the cell-culture literature, including routine short tandem repeat profiling, mycoplasma testing, and careful recording of source and passage metadata ref [13]. For HMC3, explicit reporting of repository accession, receipt route, and authentication status is not a trivial methodological detail; it is necessary to interpret discrepancies in transcriptomic, inflammatory, and phagocytic phenotypes across laboratories.

subsections.section_title: Historical Development, Identity, and Nomenclature of the HMC3 Cell Line
subsections.subsection_title: Position of HMC3 among human microglial models
subsections.content:
Within the landscape of human microglial models, HMC3 occupies an intermediate position between experimentally convenient immortalized lines and more physiologically faithful primary or stem-cell-derived systems. Its principal advantages are human origin, ease of culture, and broad availability, which have made it a common platform for mechanistic studies of inflammatory signaling, neurotoxicity, and microglia–tumor interactions. However, transcriptomic benchmarking studies have shown that immortalized microglial lines generally reproduce only part of the adult human microglial signature and tend to diverge from ex vivo microglia in genes linked to homeostatic surveillance and tissue adaptation ref [14], ref [15].

Accordingly, HMC3 is best understood as a pragmatic reductionist model rather than a stand-in for bona fide adult brain microglia. Compared with acutely isolated human microglia, it lacks the full imprint of the CNS microenvironment; compared with induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived microglia, it is less developmentally informative but usually simpler and more scalable for routine assays. Recent reviews of human microglial modeling therefore place immortalized lines such as HMC3 alongside primary cultures, monocyte-derived microglia-like cells, and iPSC-based systems as complementary tools, each suited to different experimental questions rather than a single hierarchy of quality ref [16], ref [17].

For survey readers, the key implication is comparative interpretation: results obtained in HMC3 are often valuable for hypothesis generation and controlled perturbation studies, but they should ideally be cross-validated in higher-fidelity human microglial models when claims concern microglial identity, disease-state transitions, or translational relevance.

subsections.section_title: Molecular, Phenotypic, and Functional Characterization of HMC3
subsections.content:
Assessment of HMC3 as a microglial model begins with the extent to which it retains markers commonly used to define human microglia. Early characterization of the human embryonic microglial clone 3 line reported expression of macrophage/microglia-associated antigens including CD68 and HLA-DR, supporting a myeloid identity but not, by itself, a fully homeostatic microglial phenotype ref [7]. This distinction is important because several markers once considered broadly “microglial,” such as IBA1/AIF1 or CD11b, are shared with peripheral macrophages and therefore have limited specificity for bona fide CNS-resident microglia.

More recent work has emphasized a narrower set of human microglial signature markers, notably TMEM119, P2RY12, and Sall1, which distinguish resident microglia from infiltrating monocytes/macrophages in tissue and transcriptomic datasets ref [18], ref [19]. Against this benchmark, HMC3 appears only partially representative: studies commonly detect pan-myeloid markers, whereas expression of the core homeostatic microglial signature is weak, variable, or condition-dependent at baseline. Thus, marker-based validation of HMC3 should avoid relying on generic myeloid antigens alone and instead explicitly test for these more discriminating microglial identifiers.

In practical terms, the canonical marker profile of HMC3 is best viewed as indicating an immortalized human microglia-like cell line rather than an exact surrogate for adult homeostatic microglia. This does not preclude its use, but it means that experiments sensitive to microglial identity state should document marker status under the specific culture conditions employed, ideally including both shared myeloid markers and human microglia-enriched markers ref [18], ref [19].

subsections.section_title: Molecular, Phenotypic, and Functional Characterization of HMC3
subsections.content:
Transcriptomic and proteomic studies generally place HMC3 closer to an immortalized myeloid cell state than to fully homeostatic adult human microglia. Comparative analyses of microglial model systems have shown that widely used human lines, including HMC3, express core immune and lysosomal programs but incompletely reproduce the signature genes that distinguish primary microglia in the CNS environment, particularly modules linked to TGF-β-dependent homeostasis and purinergic sensing ref [20], ref [14]. This pattern is consistent with the broader observation that microglial identity is strongly shaped by tissue context and is eroded in culture.

At the protein level, HMC3 retains abundant expression of general microglia/macrophage-associated molecules, including antigen-presentation, cytoskeletal, and stress-response proteins, but published datasets indicate attenuation or variability of more discriminative microglial markers when compared with ex vivo human microglia ref [14], ref [21]. Proteomic and transcriptomic profiles also suggest a bias toward basal proliferative and metabolic programs expected of SV40-immortalized cells, which should be considered when interpreting pathways related to cell cycle control, interferon signaling, or inflammatory priming.

Overall, available omics evidence supports using HMC3 for mechanistic studies of generic innate immune signaling, but it argues against treating the line as a faithful proxy for the full homeostatic transcriptome or proteome of human microglia. Accordingly, conclusions about disease-associated microglial states are best strengthened by benchmarking HMC3 findings against primary human microglia, iPSC-derived microglia, or human brain single-cell reference atlases ref [20], ref [22].

subsections.section_title: Molecular, Phenotypic, and Functional Characterization of HMC3
subsections.content:
Under standard monoculture conditions, HMC3 cells typically display an adherent, flattened morphology with bipolar or multipolar processes rather than the highly ramified arborization characteristic of surveillant microglia in intact brain tissue. This appearance is consistent with the long-recognized tendency of immortalized microglial lines to adopt a partially activated or culture-adapted phenotype, shaped by serum exposure, rigid plastic substrates, and absence of neuronal and astrocytic cues ref [23]. Consequently, morphology alone suggests that HMC3 more closely models a simplified in vitro basal state than fully homeostatic human microglia.

The basal cellular state of HMC3 should therefore be interpreted as intermediate: the line retains macrophage/microglia-like adherence, process formation, and viability in routine culture, yet lacks the environmental context required for a truly quiescent, finely ramified phenotype. Work revisiting the identity and properties of commonly used human microglial lines has also emphasized that HMC3/CHME3 cells show serum-culture-associated features and do not fully recapitulate primary human microglial homeostasis ref [24]. More broadly, comparisons between cultured and ex vivo human microglia indicate that withdrawal from the CNS milieu rapidly alters cell shape and basal transcriptional state, reinforcing the view that HMC3 morphology reflects adaptation to in vitro conditions as much as intrinsic microglial biology ref [25].

subsections.section_title: Molecular, Phenotypic, and Functional Characterization of HMC3
subsections.content:
HMC3 cells are inflammatory-responsive, but their behavior is best viewed as a stimulus-dependent, partial approximation of human microglial activation rather than a faithful recapitulation of in vivo state transitions. In the original characterization, the line responded to pro-inflammatory cues including lipopolysaccharide by altering cytokine-associated outputs and immune-related phenotypes, supporting its use for induced inflammatory assays ref [26]. Subsequent work has reinforced that HMC3 can mount measurable responses to canonical danger signals, yet the amplitude and breadth of these responses are often more limited than those described for primary human microglia.

The frequently used M1/M2 framework should therefore be applied cautiously in HMC3. As in microglia more broadly, activation states are not cleanly binary, and HMC3 typically exhibits mixed or incomplete polarization-like programs depending on the stimulus, exposure time, and serum context. This caveat is consistent with the broader reassessment of microglial polarization terminology and with transcriptomic evidence that cultured human microglial models diverge from homeostatic brain-resident states while retaining inducible inflammatory modules ref [2,3].

Practically, HMC3 is most informative for comparative studies of relative inflammatory signaling—for example, NF-kB-linked responses, cytokine induction, and modulation by toxic, metabolic, or pharmacologic perturbations—rather than for assigning definitive in vivo-like microglial phenotypes. Data from this line are therefore best interpreted alongside primary-cell or iPSC-derived microglial benchmarks, especially when conclusions hinge on disease-relevant activation states ref [3,4].

subsections.section_title: Molecular, Phenotypic, and Functional Characterization of HMC3
subsections.subsection_title: Phagocytosis, migration, and immune surveillance functions
subsections.content:
A key criterion for judging HMC3 as a microglial model is whether it retains the core surveillance behaviors of professional CNS macrophages. Available studies indicate that HMC3 can internalize particulate substrates and respond to inflammatory cues with altered motility-related phenotypes, but these functions are typically demonstrated under simplified in vitro conditions and at lower resolution than in primary human microglia. In the original characterization of the line, Janabi and colleagues reported phagocytic activity together with cytokine responsiveness, supporting the view that HMC3 preserves at least a partial innate immune effector program ref [29].

Subsequent work has used HMC3 in assays of migration, invasion, and stimulus-dependent immune activation, especially in tumor–microglia coculture systems. These studies generally show that HMC3 cells are chemoresponsive and can be polarized toward phenotypes associated with enhanced migration and trophic support rather than robust homeostatic surveillance, emphasizing context dependence of their behavior ref [30]. At the same time, the broad literature on microglial biology underscores that authentic immune surveillance involves highly dynamic process extension, environmental sampling, and receptor systems such as P2RY12 that are often attenuated in immortalized lines ref [27].

Overall, HMC3 is useful for comparative studies of engulfment, chemotaxis, and microglia–target cell interactions, but the line should be interpreted as modeling a reduced and partly activated version of human microglial surveillance function rather than the full repertoire of ramified, homeostatic immune monitoring seen in situ ref [1,3].

subsections.section_title: Molecular, Phenotypic, and Functional Characterization of HMC3
subsections.content:
Compared with primary human microglia, the metabolic state of HMC3 remains only partially defined, but available evidence suggests a broadly stress-adapted, continuously proliferative phenotype rather than a fully homeostatic one. This is consistent with the general principle that microglial activation is tightly coupled to immunometabolic remodeling, including shifts between oxidative phosphorylation and glycolysis, mitochondrial reactive oxygen species production, and altered redox handling under inflammatory challenge ref [31]. In practice, HMC3 is therefore best interpreted as a line in which metabolic readouts may reflect both microglial biology and adaptations imposed by immortalization and long-term culture.

Stress-response pathways are nonetheless experimentally tractable in HMC3. The line has been used to model oxidative and inflammatory injury, with changes in viability, cytokine output, and redox-sensitive signaling after exposure to agents such as lipopolysaccharide, amyloid-related stimuli, or oxidants. More broadly, transcriptomic analyses comparing immortalized human microglial lines with induced pluripotent stem cell-derived microglia have emphasized that transformed lines show substantial divergence in pathways linked to metabolism, cell cycle control, and stress signaling, reinforcing the need for caution when extrapolating basal metabolic phenotypes from HMC3 to adult human microglia ref [32].

Accordingly, HMC3 can be useful for mechanistic studies of cellular stress, mitochondrial perturbation, and neuroinflammation-associated metabolic responses, but conclusions about homeostatic microglial energetics, lipid handling, or age-related metabolic specialization should ideally be benchmarked against primary or stem cell-derived human microglial models ref [2,3].

subsections.section_title: Experimental Applications of HMC3 in Neuroinflammation and Neurological Disease Research
subsections.content:
Within the HMC3 literature, neuroinflammation and innate immune signaling constitute one of the most common application areas, because the line provides a tractable human microglial context for probing stimulus-induced cytokine production, pattern-recognition pathways, and glia-relevant stress responses. Although HMC3 does not fully recapitulate the transcriptomic state of primary human microglia, it has nevertheless been used to model canonical inflammatory outputs downstream of innate immune activation, including NF-κB-linked transcriptional programs and secretion of mediators such as IL-6, IL-8, TNF-α, and chemokines ref [34], ref [35].

A recurrent use of HMC3 has been the dissection of responses to bacterial endotoxin and other inflammatory triggers. LPS exposure in HMC3 induces broad inflammatory remodeling and has been exploited to evaluate anti-inflammatory compounds and signaling intermediates that regulate cytokine release, oxidative stress, and polarization-associated markers ref [35], ref [36]. These studies are methodologically important because they position HMC3 as a reductionist platform for testing how innate receptor engagement is coupled to downstream transcriptional and metabolic responses in human microglia-like cells.

HMC3 has also been incorporated into more complex inflammatory paradigms involving intercellular communication. In tri-culture and conditioned-medium systems, the line has been used to examine how microglia contribute to neuroinflammatory crosstalk with astrocytes and neurons, including amplification of cytokine signaling and secondary neurotoxic effects ref [37]. Taken together, this body of work supports the continued use of HMC3 as a pragmatic, if simplified, model for screening innate immune mechanisms and modulators relevant to microglia-driven neuroinflammation.

subsections.section_title: Experimental Applications of HMC3 in Neuroinflammation and Neurological Disease Research
subsections.content:
HMC3 has been used as a reductionist human microglial model to examine how disease-associated protein aggregates and neuronal stressors reshape microglial inflammatory programs relevant to neurodegeneration. In this context, the line is most often employed to quantify cytokine release, oxidative stress responses, phagocytic behavior, and signaling through pathways such as NF-κB and inflammasome-related cascades after exposure to amyloid-β, α-synuclein, or degenerating-neuron conditioned media. Although HMC3 does not fully reproduce the transcriptional state of primary adult microglia, its human origin and experimental tractability have made it useful for initial mechanistic screening in Alzheimer’s- and Parkinson’s-related paradigms.

In Alzheimer’s disease-oriented studies, HMC3 has been incorporated into amyloid-β challenge systems to probe inflammatory activation and microglia-neuron crosstalk, often alongside neuronal cell lines or mixed co-culture designs. Such work aligns with broader evidence that human microglia exposed to amyloidogenic stimuli adopt reactive states linked to cytokine production and neurotoxicity ref [38]. The cell line has also been used to test whether candidate therapeutics attenuate amyloid-triggered inflammatory outputs, thereby serving as an intermediate platform between simplified biochemical assays and more complex primary-cell or in vivo models.

Beyond amyloid biology, HMC3 has been applied to synucleinopathy-relevant questions, including responses to extracellular α-synuclein species and the propagation of inflammatory injury in neuron–microglia systems. This usage is conceptually supported by studies showing that aggregated α-synuclein can directly activate microglia and amplify neurodegenerative cascades ref [39], and by transcriptomic work defining disease-associated microglial states in human neurodegenerative conditions ref [19]. Accordingly, HMC3 is best viewed as a pragmatic discovery tool for dissecting conserved microglial effector mechanisms, with findings ideally validated in induced pluripotent stem cell-derived or primary human microglia.

subsections.section_title: Experimental Applications of HMC3 in Neuroinflammation and Neurological Disease Research
subsections.subsection_title: Brain tumor and tumor microenvironment studies
subsections.content:
HMC3 has been used in brain tumor research primarily as a tractable human microglial model for studying how neoplastic cells reprogram resident innate immune populations within the glioma microenvironment. In this setting, investigators have exploited HMC3 to examine tumor-conditioned polarization, chemotactic recruitment, and the acquisition of immunoregulatory phenotypes that resemble glioma-associated microglia/macrophages. Such work aligns with the broader view that glioblastoma-derived signals actively convert microglia toward states that support invasion, angiogenesis, and immune suppression rather than anti-tumor surveillance ref [40], ref [41].

Experimentally, HMC3 has been incorporated into co-culture and conditioned-medium paradigms with glioblastoma cells to probe reciprocal signaling through cytokines, growth factors, and extracellular vesicle-associated cargo. These studies are particularly useful for dissecting how tumor-secreted mediators alter microglial expression of inflammatory genes, matrix-remodeling programs, and migratory behavior, while also allowing assessment of how microglia-derived factors feed back on glioma proliferation and invasiveness. This application is conceptually supported by transcriptomic and functional analyses showing that glioma-associated myeloid cells occupy distinct, tumor-educated states within human disease and contribute materially to malignant progression ref [41], ref [42].

Although HMC3 cannot recapitulate the full ontogeny or heterogeneity of primary human microglia, its use in tumor microenvironment studies remains valuable for mechanism-oriented screening, especially when paired with orthogonal validation in primary cells, organotypic systems, or patient-derived models. Accordingly, HMC3-based experiments have served as reductionist platforms for identifying candidate microglia-targeted interventions aimed at disrupting pro-tumor inflammation or restoring immune effector functions in glioma ref [40], ref [43].

subsections.section_title: Experimental Applications of HMC3 in Neuroinflammation and Neurological Disease Research
subsections.subsection_title: Viral, bacterial, and other infectious disease contexts
subsections.content:
Although HMC3 has been used less extensively in infection biology than in sterile neuroinflammation, it has served as a tractable human microglial platform for probing pathogen-triggered innate immune responses. In viral contexts, HMC3 has been employed to examine how neurotropic or inflammation-inducing agents reshape microglial cytokine programs, oxidative stress, and antiviral signaling, complementing primary-cell and iPSC-derived microglia models. For example, studies of Zika virus infection in human microglial cell systems, including HMC3/C16-related platforms, showed productive infection accompanied by inflammatory activation and highlighted microglia as potential CNS reservoirs and amplifiers of neuropathogenesis ref [44].

HMC3 has also been incorporated into bacterial and mixed host-pathogen paradigms that focus on innate sensing rather than direct microbial replication. In these settings, exposure to bacterial endotoxin or pathogen-associated molecular patterns is used to model microglial activation states relevant to sepsis-associated encephalopathy, meningitic inflammation, or chronic neuroimmune priming. Such applications are conceptually aligned with broader evidence that human microglia-like cell lines mount NF-kappaB-linked cytokine responses and exhibit altered phagocytic and metabolic behavior after inflammatory challenge ref [45].

More recently, infectious-disease applications have expanded toward virus-associated neurodegeneration and host-factor studies. During the COVID-19 era, human microglial models including HMC3 were used to investigate SARS-CoV-2 spike- or virus-associated inflammatory signaling, apoptosis-related pathways, and crosstalk with neural cells, supporting the view that microglia may contribute to indirect CNS injury even when robust productive infection is limited ref [46]. Overall, these studies position HMC3 as a useful reductionist system for dissecting microglial responses to infectious stimuli, while underscoring the need for validation in more physiologic human microglia models.

subsections.section_title: Experimental Applications of HMC3 in Neuroinflammation and Neurological Disease Research
subsections.content:
HMC3 has also been used as a tractable human microglial model for neurotoxicity and environmental exposure studies, particularly when the aim is to resolve how xenobiotics or stress-associated chemicals reprogram innate immune signaling. In this context, the line is valuable for separating direct microglial responses from neuron-dependent secondary effects, including shifts in cytokine release, redox balance, and inflammatory transcriptional programs that may contribute to bystander neurotoxicity.

A representative application is the analysis of microglial responses to endocrine-disrupting and industrial chemicals. Exposure paradigms using bisphenol A have shown that human microglial cells can mount a measurable pro-inflammatory response, with increased expression of mediators such as IL-6 and TNF-α and evidence for involvement of estrogen receptor-related signaling pathways, supporting the use of HMC3-like systems to interrogate environmentally driven microglial activation ref [47]. Related work on toxicant-triggered inflammatory priming in human microglia has further emphasized oxidative stress and NF-κB-linked signaling as recurring mechanisms by which non-neuronal brain cells translate chemical exposure into neuroinflammatory outputs ref [48].

More broadly, these studies position HMC3 as a useful screening platform for identifying compounds that do not simply kill microglia, but instead bias them toward persistent inflammatory or stress-reactive states. This is particularly relevant for environmental risk assessment, where low-dose or chronic exposures may alter microglial phenotype and thereby modulate susceptibility to later neurodegenerative or injury-related insults rather than producing overt acute cytotoxicity ref [48], ref [49].

subsections.section_title: Experimental Applications of HMC3 in Neuroinflammation and Neurological Disease Research
subsections.content:
Although HMC3 has been used less extensively in aging and repair biology than in inflammatory stimulation paradigms, it has nevertheless served as a tractable human microglial model for studying how chronic stressors shift microglia toward phenotypes relevant to tissue vulnerability, impaired homeostasis, and defective recovery. In this context, work using serum deprivation, oxidative challenge, and altered trophic support has highlighted the sensitivity of HMC3 cells to pathways governing survival, mitochondrial function, and inflammatory reprogramming, features that are closely linked to age-associated microglial dysfunction and reduced reparative capacity in the CNS ref [50].

HMC3 has also been incorporated into injury-oriented in vitro systems that probe microglial responses to damage-associated signals and neuron- or glia-derived distress cues. Such studies are useful for dissecting processes that lie at the interface of degeneration and repair, including cytokine release, phagocytic behavior, and crosstalk with astrocytes or tumor-derived factors. More broadly, the line’s transcriptomic and proteomic characterization has helped define both its utility and its limitations for modeling homeostatic versus activated microglial states, an important consideration when interpreting findings related to aging, wound resolution, and regenerative signaling ref [51], ref [52].

subsections.section_title: Culture Conditions, Experimental Design, and Analytical Methodologies
subsections.subsection_title: Standard culture media and maintenance protocols
subsections.content:
Standard maintenance of HMC3 cells remains closely tied to the conditions reported for the original human fetal microglial line from which the clone was derived. Early descriptions used Eagle’s minimum essential medium supplemented with fetal bovine serum and glutamine, with routine propagation as an adherent monolayer under conventional humidified 5% CO2 culture conditions; these baseline parameters continue to influence how the line is handled in later studies, even when nomenclature shifted from CHME3 to HMC3 ref [4]. Because HMC3 is immortalized with SV40 large T antigen, passage-dependent drift, changes in proliferation rate, and altered inflammatory responsiveness are plausible concerns, making careful tracking of passage number and medium composition particularly important ref [4], ref [53].

In practice, however, substantial heterogeneity exists across laboratories. HMC3 has been maintained not only in EMEM/MEM-based formulations but also in DMEM or DMEM/F12 variants, typically with 5–10% fetal bovine serum, antibiotics, and variable use of non-essential amino acids, sodium pyruvate, or glutamine supplements. Such differences are not trivial: serum concentration and basal nutrient composition can alter resting morphology, growth kinetics, and the apparent magnitude of cytokine-induced activation, thereby complicating cross-study comparison. Authentication and contamination control are also essential, as HMC3 is distributed through cell repositories with defined handling recommendations and has been the subject of transcriptomic and proteomic characterization that underscores the importance of standardized baseline culture states before stimulation ref [53], ref [54].

For survey purposes, the key methodological point is that reporting of medium brand/formulation, serum source and percentage, coating conditions if used, seeding density, passage window, and recovery time after thawing should be treated as core experimental variables rather than routine details. Greater adherence to repository guidance and explicit reporting standards would improve reproducibility and help distinguish true biological effects from culture-condition-dependent shifts in HMC3 phenotype ref [54], ref [55].

subsections.section_title: Culture Conditions, Experimental Design, and Analytical Methodologies
subsections.content:
Stimulation protocols are a major source of variability in HMC3 studies because they determine both the amplitude and the phenotype of the measured response. Most work uses acute inflammatory challenges—especially lipopolysaccharide (LPS), tumor necrosis factor-α, interleukin-1β, interferon-γ, or combinations thereof—but concentrations, serum conditions, and exposure windows vary markedly across laboratories. This is consequential because human microglia often respond differently from rodent microglia to canonical innate immune ligands, and immortalized lines can display attenuated or context-dependent Toll-like receptor signaling relative to primary cells ref [56].

Treatment variables also shape interpretation of downstream endpoints. Short stimulations are commonly used to capture NF-κB activation, cytokine transcription, or rapid metabolic changes, whereas 24–72 h paradigms are more likely to reveal effects on viability, phagocytosis, oxidative stress, and morphology. Polarization-style designs that classify responses as “M1/M2” remain common, yet this framework incompletely reflects the multidimensional activation states observed in human microglia and can oversimplify HMC3 phenotypes ref [27]. Accordingly, reporting should include agonist source and purity, vehicle composition, dose range, exposure duration, and whether treatments are applied in complete, serum-reduced, or serum-free medium.

A further consideration is the use of disease-relevant stimuli rather than only generic inflammatory triggers. HMC3 cells have been challenged with amyloid-β species, α-synuclein assemblies, HIV-associated proteins, hypoxia/reoxygenation, and conditioned media from tumor or neural cultures to model neurodegenerative, infectious, and neuro-oncology contexts. Such paradigms may improve translational relevance, but they also introduce additional variables—including aggregation state, endotoxin contamination, and lot-to-lot heterogeneity—that should be standardized and explicitly documented ref [57], ref [58].

subsections.section_title: Culture Conditions, Experimental Design, and Analytical Methodologies
subsections.content:
Most HMC3 studies still rely on conventional two-dimensional monolayers because they are inexpensive, scalable, and compatible with microscopy, cytokine assays, and transcript or protein profiling. However, substrate chemistry, serum exposure, and plating density can substantially alter baseline morphology and inflammatory tone, making direct comparison across laboratories difficult. More broadly, the limitations of immortalized human microglial monocultures in 2D have been emphasized by transcriptomic benchmarking studies showing that culture context strongly influences how closely in vitro microglia resemble ex vivo states ref [59].

Three-dimensional systems seek to mitigate some of these constraints by embedding microglia-like cells within extracellular matrix gels, spheroids, or brain organoid environments that better reproduce cell-cell contact, diffusion gradients, and ramified morphology. In related human microglial modeling, incorporation of microglia into cerebral organoids has revealed context-dependent maturation and surveillance phenotypes that are not readily captured in flat monoculture ref [60]. Although such studies are not always performed with HMC3 specifically, they illustrate the direction of more physiologically relevant platforms against which HMC3-based 3D adaptations can be evaluated.

Co-culture designs are especially important for HMC3 because many disease-relevant responses depend on reciprocal signaling with astrocytes, neurons, endothelial cells, or glioma cells. Tri-culture and barrier models have shown that microglial inflammatory outputs are reshaped by neighboring CNS cell types and by paracrine versus contact-dependent interactions ref [3,4]. For HMC3, these configurations are therefore useful not only for mechanistic studies but also for identifying which phenotypes are intrinsic to the line and which emerge only within multicellular microenvironments.

subsections.section_title: Culture Conditions, Experimental Design, and Analytical Methodologies
subsections.subsection_title: Readouts for viability, activation, and function
subsections.content:
Readouts used in HMC3 studies typically span three partially overlapping domains: viability/cell health, inflammatory activation state, and effector function. Viability is most often assessed with metabolic assays such as MTT, WST-1, resazurin/Alamar Blue, or ATP-based luminescence, frequently complemented by LDH release, Annexin V/propidium iodide staining, or caspase measurements to distinguish cytotoxicity from apoptosis or secondary necrosis. Because microglial activation can itself alter mitochondrial metabolism and redox state, metabolic assays should be interpreted cautiously and ideally paired with direct cell counting or membrane-integrity measurements.

Activation is commonly inferred from changes in morphology, surface markers, and secreted mediators. HMC3 cells are often evaluated for ramified-to-amoeboid morphological shifts, altered IBA1/AIF1, CD11b, CD68, HLA-DR, or MHC-related markers, and induction of cytokines such as IL-1beta, IL-6, TNF-alpha, and chemokines measured by qPCR, ELISA, or multiplex immunoassays. Broad experience with human microglial models indicates that immortalized lines can show stimulus-dependent and sometimes attenuated inflammatory responses relative to primary microglia, making marker panels and stimulus timing critical for interpretation ref [63], ref [64].

Functional assays provide a more mechanistic layer of phenotyping. Common endpoints include phagocytosis of fluorescent beads or labeled amyloid material, ROS/NO production, calcium signaling, migration in scratch or transwell formats, and pathway-specific readouts such as NF-kappaB nuclear translocation. Reviews of microglial methodology emphasize that no single assay adequately captures microglial state; multimodal designs that combine viability, cytokine profiling, and functional measurements are therefore better suited to comparing HMC3 responses across laboratories ref [27], ref [65].

subsections.section_title: Culture Conditions, Experimental Design, and Analytical Methodologies
subsections.content:
Omics and imaging workflows offer an important route for moving beyond a narrow panel of inflammatory readouts in HMC3 studies. Transcriptomic profiling can capture broad shifts in cytokine signaling, interferon programs, lipid metabolism, and cell-cycle state, but interpretation requires caution because immortalized microglial lines may diverge from primary or ex vivo human microglia under basal conditions and after stimulation ref [14], ref [66]. Consequently, HMC3 omics datasets are often most informative for within-model perturbational comparisons rather than for direct claims about human microglial identity.

High-content microscopy complements bulk molecular assays by resolving morphology, subcellular trafficking, and cell-to-cell heterogeneity. In HMC3 cultures, multiparametric imaging of soma size, process complexity, nuclear texture, lysosomal compartments, mitochondrial potential, and marker localization can distinguish cytotoxicity from activation-like phenotypes and can reveal mixed responses that would be obscured in averaged biochemical assays. The broader microglial imaging literature also shows that standardized image-analysis pipelines are essential, because activation-associated morphological transitions are highly sensitive to plating density, serum exposure, and segmentation strategy ref [67].

For analytical rigor, omics and imaging datasets should be normalized with explicit attention to batch, passage number, and stimulation timing, and ideally benchmarked against external human microglial references. Integrative frameworks that combine transcriptomics with single-cell or spatially resolved imaging are especially valuable for HMC3, where population averaging can mask substantial phenotypic drift. As emphasized in human microglia benchmarking studies, transparent reporting of preprocessing, feature selection, and reference standards is critical for cross-study comparability ref [14], ref [66], ref [68].

subsections.section_title: Culture Conditions, Experimental Design, and Analytical Methodologies
subsections.subsection_title: Data normalization, reproducibility, and reporting quality
subsections.content:
For HMC3 studies, data normalization is a major determinant of interpretability because readouts are highly sensitive to passage number, plating density, serum exposure, basal activation state, and assay timing. Simple normalization to untreated controls is often insufficient when treatments also alter cell number or metabolic activity; in such cases, cytokine secretion, phagocytosis, ROS, or transcript abundance should ideally be indexed to independently measured cell counts, protein content, or viability metrics. The broader preclinical reproducibility literature has emphasized that inadequate handling of biological and technical variation can inflate apparent effects and hinder cross-study comparison ref [69].

Reproducibility also depends on rigorous cell-line authentication and contamination control. HMC3 is frequently used as an immortalized human microglial model, but immortalized lines are vulnerable to drift, misidentification, and mycoplasma-associated transcriptomic artifacts, making routine STR profiling, mycoplasma testing, and explicit reporting of source, lot, and passage essential. Community standards for cell line validation and documentation therefore apply directly to HMC3 workflows and should be regarded as minimum reporting requirements rather than optional quality measures ref [70], ref [71].

Reporting quality can be improved by adopting structured disclosure of experimental design features: exact medium formulation, serum percentage, confluence at treatment, duration of preconditioning, stimulant preparation, replicate definitions, exclusion criteria, and statistical unit. In addition, transcriptomic or high-content studies should report batch-correction strategy, normalization method, and deposition of raw data and metadata. Such practices align with broader principles for transparent and reproducible preclinical reporting, including explicit attention to randomization, blinding where feasible, and a priori definition of primary outcomes ref [72].

subsections.section_title: Strengths, Limitations, and Interpretive Challenges of the HMC3 Model
subsections.subsection_title: Advantages of accessibility and experimental tractability
subsections.content:
A major advantage of HMC3 is practical accessibility. Unlike primary human microglia, which are limited by donor availability, variable tissue quality, and difficult isolation procedures, HMC3 can be expanded reproducibly, shared across laboratories, and maintained with standard cell culture methods. This lowers technical barriers for microglial experiments and enables routine use in laboratories that lack access to fresh human brain tissue. The line’s human origin and immortalized growth properties have therefore made it a convenient platform for exploratory studies of inflammatory signaling, toxicant exposure, and neuron–glia interactions under controlled conditions ref [4].

Its experimental tractability is especially valuable for reductionist and medium-throughput designs. HMC3 cells permit straightforward perturbation with cytokines, pathogen-associated stimuli, drugs, or genetic manipulations, while minimizing the donor-to-donor heterogeneity that complicates interpretation in primary cultures. They are also compatible with common readouts such as transcript and protein profiling, migration and phagocytosis assays, and co-culture systems. In this sense, HMC3 occupies a useful niche similar to other widely used microglial cell lines, which have historically facilitated mechanistic screening before validation in more physiologically faithful models ref [73], ref [74].

Accordingly, HMC3 is best viewed as an efficient first-pass human microglial surrogate: it is well suited for hypothesis generation, protocol development, and comparative perturbation studies in which reproducibility and scalability are priorities. These logistical strengths help explain its continued use despite well-recognized limitations in faithfully recapitulating adult homeostatic human microglia.

subsections.section_title: Strengths, Limitations, and Interpretive Challenges of the HMC3 Model
subsections.content:
A central limitation of HMC3 is that it does not fully reproduce the transcriptional and functional identity of primary human microglia. Primary microglia are shaped by a CNS-specific milieu, including TGF-β, CSF1/IL-34 signaling, neuronal contact, and region-specific cues, and removal from this environment rapidly alters their state ref [75]. In immortalized lines such as HMC3, this problem is compounded by long-term adaptation to serum-containing culture, which tends to favor a generalized myeloid phenotype over the homeostatic microglial program seen in freshly isolated human cells.

Comparative studies of human microglia have shown that canonical homeostatic markers and regulatory networks are difficult to maintain ex vivo and are often diminished relative to acutely isolated cells ref [76], ref [14]. This is important for interpreting HMC3 data because responses involving surveillance, synaptic remodeling, lipid metabolism, or disease-associated state transitions may depend on molecular programs that are weakly represented or absent in the cell line. Accordingly, HMC3 can model selected inflammatory or toxic responses, but it should not be assumed to capture the full repertoire of adult human microglial phenotypes observed in vivo.

subsections.section_title: Strengths, Limitations, and Interpretive Challenges of the HMC3 Model
subsections.subsection_title: Effects of immortalization, passage number, and drift
subsections.content:
A central interpretive issue for HMC3 is that immortalization can stabilize growth at the cost of altering core microglial programs. Immortalized human microglial lines were originally generated to overcome the scarcity and limited lifespan of primary cells, but transformation and long-term adaptation may reshape cell-cycle control, stress responses, and inflammatory signaling, making it difficult to disentangle microglia-relevant biology from line-specific effects ref [77]. This concern is consistent with broader analyses showing that cultured or transformed microglia diverge substantially from ex vivo human and murine microglia in transcriptional identity, especially for homeostatic genes that depend on CNS context ref [78].

Passage number adds a second layer of variability. With repeated expansion, immortalized lines can undergo phenotypic drift, including changes in morphology, proliferation rate, basal cytokine tone, and responsiveness to stimuli. Such drift may arise through clonal selection, epigenetic remodeling, or gradual adaptation to serum-containing media and rigid plastic substrates. In practice, this means that HMC3 results obtained at different passage windows may not be directly comparable unless passage history, thawing strategy, and culture duration are tightly controlled and reported.

These issues do not render HMC3 unusable, but they narrow the strength of inference. Experiments focused on relative perturbation responses within a single, well-documented passage range are generally more defensible than claims about stable human microglial identity or in vivo-state fidelity. Routine authentication, mycoplasma testing, banking of early-passage stocks, and periodic benchmarking against primary or stem cell-derived human microglia are therefore essential safeguards when using HMC3 as a surrogate model ref [78], ref [79].

subsections.section_title: Strengths, Limitations, and Interpretive Challenges of the HMC3 Model
subsections.subsection_title: Context dependence and loss of tissue-specific cues
subsections.content:
A central limitation of HMC3 is that microglial identity is highly context dependent. In vivo, microglia are continuously instructed by the CNS niche through cell-cell contact, extracellular matrix composition, neuronal activity, and soluble factors such as TGF-β, IL-34, and CSF1. Removal from this environment drives rapid erosion of the homeostatic program in both rodent and human microglia, with reduced expression of canonical genes and altered inflammatory responsiveness, indicating that culture systems intrinsically reshape phenotype rather than merely preserving a pre-existing state ref [80], ref [81].

This issue is especially relevant for HMC3 because immortalized monocultures lack the layered spatial and developmental cues that distinguish microglia across brain regions, ages, and disease states. Transcriptomic analyses have shown that even freshly isolated human microglia differ substantially from ex vivo or in vitro counterparts, underscoring how strongly local CNS signals govern their state ref [82]. Consequently, HMC3 responses to cytokines, amyloid-related stimuli, pathogens, or toxicants should be interpreted as outputs of a decontextualized myeloid-like system rather than direct readouts of tissue-embedded human microglia.

The practical implication is not that HMC3 is unusable, but that experimental conclusions should be bounded by the absence of niche instruction. HMC3 may still be informative for reductionist studies of signaling, screening, or perturbation ranking, whereas questions involving microglial homeostasis, region-specific specialization, neuron-glia reciprocity, or disease-associated state transitions are particularly vulnerable to artifacts arising from loss of tissue-specific cues.

subsections.section_title: Strengths, Limitations, and Interpretive Challenges of the HMC3 Model
subsections.content:
A persistent challenge in interpreting the HMC3 literature is substantial inter-study variability in baseline phenotype and stimulus responsiveness. Reports differ on expression of canonical microglial markers, inflammatory amplitude, phagocytic behavior, and sensitivity to toxic protein aggregates, making direct comparison across studies difficult. Some of this inconsistency reflects broader problems in human microglial models: transcriptomic analyses have shown that cultured microglia rapidly diverge from ex vivo states, losing key homeostatic signatures and adopting context-dependent stress or activation programs ref [83]. In an immortalized line such as HMC3, these shifts are likely compounded by laboratory-specific culture histories.

Methodological heterogeneity further amplifies discordant findings. Differences in serum exposure, substrate, passage number, authentication status, mycoplasma testing, and even nomenclature can alter the apparent phenotype of transformed microglial lines. Reviews of immortalized human microglia have emphasized that HMC3 has been used under widely varying conditions, often without sufficient reporting of provenance or culture parameters, which limits reproducibility and encourages overgeneralization ref [84]. More generally, concerns about cell line misidentification and cross-contamination remain relevant when comparing older studies with recent work ref [70].

Accordingly, apparent contradictions in the HMC3 literature should not always be interpreted as biological disagreement. Rather, they often indicate that HMC3 is highly state-dependent and experimentally plastic. Standardized reporting, routine authentication, and side-by-side benchmarking against primary or iPSC-derived human microglia are therefore essential if results obtained in HMC3 are to be synthesized reliably across laboratories.

subsections.section_title: Strengths, Limitations, and Interpretive Challenges of the HMC3 Model
subsections.content:
HMC3 is most appropriately used as a convenient, human-derived screening platform for questions that do not require faithful reconstruction of adult homeostatic microglial identity. In practice, this includes hypothesis generation, comparative perturbation studies under tightly standardized conditions, transfection- or reporter-based assays, and first-pass testing of inflammatory signaling, toxicant responses, or microglia–tumor crosstalk where experimental tractability and reproducibility are prioritized over in vivo fidelity. Such use is justified precisely because immortalized human microglial lines offer accessibility and scalability that primary human microglia rarely provide, even though they diverge transcriptionally and functionally from bona fide microglia ref [85], ref [19].

By contrast, HMC3 is a poor stand-alone model for claims about core human microglial biology in situ, including developmental origin programs, homeostatic signature gene regulation, region-specific states, aging-associated phenotypes, and disease-associated microglial transitions that depend on brain niche signals. Work comparing cultured or transformed microglial models with ex vivo human microglia has shown that removal from the CNS environment and adaptation to in vitro growth conditions substantially reshape microglial identity ref [19], ref [86]. Accordingly, conclusions about neurodegenerative disease mechanisms, patient-specific inflammatory states, or therapeutic target validation should ideally be corroborated in primary human microglia, iPSC-derived microglia in more physiological co-culture systems, or in vivo datasets ref [86], ref [87].

A practical interpretive standard is therefore to treat HMC3 as an engineered response model rather than a definitive surrogate for human brain-resident microglia. It is useful when the question is cell-intrinsic and reductionist; it is inappropriate when the biological claim depends on tissue imprinting, multicellular circuitry, or disease-state authenticity.

subsections.section_title: Toward Best Practices and Next-Generation Human Microglial Modeling
subsections.subsection_title: Recommended standards for authentication and characterization
subsections.content:
A minimum standard for HMC3 use should begin with rigorous identity control. Investigators should report the exact source repository, lot or vial information, passage number at thawing and experimentation, routine mycoplasma testing, and short tandem repeat profiling to verify human cell identity and exclude cross-contamination, in line with broader recommendations for cell-line authentication in biomedical research ref [70]. Because immortalized microglial lines can drift substantially with passage and culture history, manuscripts should also specify serum conditions, substrate, seeding density, and exposure duration for any priming or differentiation factors.

Characterization should move beyond morphology and a small marker panel. At baseline and after perturbation, HMC3 cells should be benchmarked by transcript and protein expression of core microglial identity genes such as P2RY12, TMEM119, CX3CR1, CSF1R, AIF1, and SPI1/PU.1, while also documenting markers associated with macrophage-like deviation or activation. This recommendation follows accumulating evidence that authentic human microglial identity is defined by a distinctive transcriptional program that is highly context dependent and often attenuated in vitro ref [2,3]. Flow cytometry or immunoblotting should therefore be paired with qPCR or RNA-seq, rather than relying on IBA1 alone.

Functional validation should be reported as a compact assay set matched to study aims: phagocytosis, cytokine secretion, motility, and responses to canonical inflammatory and homeostatic cues. Wherever feasible, HMC3 outputs should be compared against primary or induced pluripotent stem cell-derived human microglia assayed under the same conditions, using recently proposed consensus marker frameworks for human microglial states ref [89]. Such standardized authentication and phenotyping would make HMC3 studies more reproducible and easier to interpret within the broader landscape of human microglial models.

subsections.section_title: Toward Best Practices and Next-Generation Human Microglial Modeling
subsections.subsection_title: Benchmarking against primary and stem cell-derived microglia
subsections.content:
Benchmarking HMC3 against primary human microglia and stem cell-derived microglia is essential because immortalization and long-term adaptation to serum culture can uncouple a line from the transcriptional and functional state of bona fide CNS-resident microglia. Comparative frameworks should therefore prioritize concordance with core human microglial identity genes, including TMEM119, P2RY12, CX3CR1, TREM2, and SALL1, while also testing inducible programs relevant to inflammation, phagocytosis, lipid handling, and interferon responses. Human transcriptomic studies have defined these reference signatures in freshly isolated microglia and provide a rational baseline for judging where HMC3 captures, or fails to capture, homeostatic identity ref [90].

Stem cell-derived systems offer a second benchmark because they can reproduce developmental ontogeny and, under appropriate cues, acquire many microglial features that are absent or attenuated in transformed lines. Protocols generating microglia-like cells from human pluripotent stem cells have established practical comparators for morphology, cytokine responsiveness, synaptic pruning-related functions, and integration into neural co-cultures or xenograft settings ref [91], ref [92]. In this context, HMC3 is likely most informative when used as a standardized, scalable perturbation model rather than as a surrogate for fully homeostatic microglia.

A best-practice benchmarking pipeline would therefore include side-by-side multi-omic profiling, standardized stimulation panels, and shared functional assays across HMC3, primary human microglia, and at least one induced pluripotent stem cell-derived microglial platform. Such benchmarking should be framed not as pass-fail validation, but as definition of the model’s domain of applicability: for example, whether HMC3 better approximates proliferative, stress-adapted, or inflammatory microglial states than quiescent adult human microglia.

subsections.section_title: Toward Best Practices and Next-Generation Human Microglial Modeling
subsections.subsection_title: Integration with organoids and blood-brain barrier models
subsections.content:
Integration of HMC3 with brain organoids and blood-brain barrier (BBB) platforms offers a practical route to move beyond monoculture phenotypes and to test how a human microglial line behaves within multicellular, spatially organized neural environments. Organoid studies have shown that incorporation of microglia-like cells can alter neuronal network maturation, synaptic remodeling, and inflammatory responsiveness, underscoring the importance of microglial context in 3D systems ref [93], ref [60]. In this setting, HMC3 can serve as a standardized comparator or pilot model for assay development, provided investigators explicitly recognize that transformed immortalized cells may not fully recapitulate developmental integration or homeostatic microglial states.

For BBB applications, co-culture with human brain endothelial cells, astrocytes, and pericytes can be used to evaluate whether HMC3 reproduces key microglia-driven barrier effects, including cytokine-mediated permeability changes, leukocyte signaling, and responses to circulating insults. Human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived BBB microvessels and organ-chip systems have established tractable benchmarks for barrier integrity and neuroimmune interaction that can guide such validation ref [94], ref [95]. Best practice is therefore to use HMC3 in these advanced platforms as a scalable perturbation tool while benchmarking transcriptomic state, secretome, motility, and barrier-modulating activity against primary or stem cell-derived microglia under matched co-culture conditions.

subsections.section_title: Toward Best Practices and Next-Generation Human Microglial Modeling
subsections.subsection_title: Use in screening, systems biology, and translational pipelines
subsections.content:
Within screening workflows, HMC3 is best viewed as a tractable first-pass human microglial platform rather than a stand-alone disease surrogate. Its advantages are scalability, batch stability, and compatibility with high-content imaging, transcript profiling, and multiplex cytokine assays, making it useful for prioritizing perturbations that modulate inflammatory tone, phagocytic behavior, oxidative stress, or microglia–tumor crosstalk. However, because immortalization and culture adaptation can uncouple HMC3 from key homeostatic programs seen in primary and stem cell-derived microglia, hits identified in HMC3 should be advanced only through staged confirmation in more physiological systems ref [96], ref [97].

For systems biology, the greatest value of HMC3 lies in comparative and perturbational designs: integrating transcriptomics, proteomics, secretomics, and phospho-signaling can map conserved response modules while also revealing where this line diverges from bona fide human microglia. Such analyses are especially informative when benchmarked against human iPSC-derived microglia and ex vivo datasets, which have clarified core human microglial signatures and context-dependent activation states ref [97], ref [15]. In translational pipelines, an efficient strategy is therefore tiered: use HMC3 for target nomination and mechanism-focused screening, then validate in iPSC-derived microglia, multicellular organoid or blood-brain barrier co-cultures, and, where feasible, primary human specimens before nominating therapeutic candidates ref [96], ref [98].

subsections.section_title: Toward Best Practices and Next-Generation Human Microglial Modeling
subsections.content:
A central unresolved question is how far HMC3 can approximate bona fide human microglial identity across experimental contexts. Microglial state is highly shaped by developmental origin, brain-region cues, age, sex, and disease environment, yet immortalized lines are removed from many of these determinants and may drift transcriptionally with passage. This concern is amplified by the broader recognition that cultured microglia rapidly lose key homeostatic signatures outside the CNS milieu, making it difficult to distinguish limitations intrinsic to HMC3 from limitations shared by in vitro systems more generally ref [79].

A second challenge is defining what constitutes an appropriate benchmark. Comparisons with primary human microglia, induced pluripotent stem cell-derived microglia, and xenotransplantation-based models often yield different conclusions depending on whether emphasis is placed on morphology, cytokine responsiveness, phagocytosis, metabolism, or transcriptomic fidelity. Recent work showing that human iPSC-derived microglia acquire more mature, context-dependent states after transplantation underscores how strongly environmental instruction shapes phenotype and highlights the uncertainty of evaluating HMC3 in simplified monoculture alone ref [99].

Unresolved technical questions also remain about reproducibility and translational interpretation. Laboratories still differ in authentication practices, media composition, serum use, inflammatory stimuli, and endpoint selection, hindering cross-study synthesis. More fundamentally, it remains unclear for which classes of questions HMC3 is sufficiently informative: broad mechanistic screening, human-specific innate immune signaling, BBB crosstalk, or disease modeling requiring state-resolved microglial programs. Addressing these gaps will require explicit fit-for-purpose frameworks, standardized multi-omic benchmarking, and routine reporting of provenance, passage, and response envelopes rather than assuming a single fixed microglial identity.

subsections.section_title: Toward Best Practices and Next-Generation Human Microglial Modeling
subsections.subsection_title: Future outlook for human microglial in vitro research
subsections.content:
The future of human microglial in vitro research will likely be defined less by any single model and more by interoperable model ecosystems. HMC3 and related immortalized lines can remain useful as scalable, perturbation-friendly platforms, but their value will increasingly depend on explicit calibration against primary human microglia and induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived counterparts under standardized molecular and functional benchmarks. Recent single-cell and xenotransplantation studies have clarified the transcriptional programs associated with bona fide human microglial identity and environmental maturation, providing a concrete reference framework for such benchmarking ref [100], ref [101].

A major next step is to move from static monocultures toward context-rich systems that preserve the reciprocal signaling shaping microglial state. Human microglia are profoundly instructed by neural, vascular, and immune niches, and organoid, assembloid, blood-brain barrier, and microphysiological systems are therefore likely to become central for modeling disease-relevant phenotypes, especially when combined with controlled perturbations and longitudinal multi-omic readouts. In parallel, CRISPR-based perturbation, high-content imaging, and single-cell profiling should enable model-specific strengths to be matched to distinct use cases rather than forcing a one-model-fits-all paradigm ref [102].

Looking ahead, the field will benefit most from community standards for provenance, passage control, media composition, and reporting of microglial identity metrics, coupled with open reference atlases and cross-laboratory benchmarking datasets. Such efforts would allow HMC3-based studies to be interpreted within a transparent continuum of model fidelity and experimental tractability, accelerating both mechanistic discovery and translational prioritization ref [103].
